results.title: 5.3 Learning Structured Graphs | Portfolio Optimization
results.content:
Title: 5.3 Learning Structured Graphs | Portfolio Optimization
A \(k\)-component graph (i.e., a graph with \(k\) clusters or components) is characterized by its Laplacian matrix being low rank with \(k\) zero eigenvalues (Chung, 1997). Example of a three-component graph (three clusters) with corresponding Laplacian matrix eigenvalues (three zero eigenvalues). * *Low-rank graph approximation*: Suppose we are given a graph in the form of a Laplacian matrix \(\bm{L}\_0\); we can formulate the low-rank approximation problem as \[\begin{equation} \begin{array}{ll} \underset{\bm{L}\succeq\bm{0}, \bm{F}}{\textm{minimize}} & \|\bm{L} - \bm{L}\_0\|\_\textm{F}^2 + \gamma \textm{Tr}\left(\bm{F}^\T\bm{L}\bm{F}\right)\\ \textm{subject to} & \bm{L}\bm{1}=\bm{0}, \quad L\_{ij} = L\_{ji} \le 0, \quad \forall i\neq j,\\ & \textm{diag}(\bm{L})=\bm{1},\\ & \bm{F}^\T\bm{F}=\bm{I}. * *Low-rank graphs from sparse GMRFs*: Consider the formulation in (5.7) to learn a sparse Laplacian matrix under a GMRF framework. Enforcing a low-rank Laplacian matrix will generate a \(k\)-component graph, but it may have isolated nodes. To avoid such trivial graph solutions one can control the degrees of the nodes with the constraint \(\textm{diag}(\bm{L})=\bm{1}\) (Cardoso and Palomar, 2020). An alternative and more convenient characterization of a bipartite graph is via its Laplacian matrix, which has the following structure:25 \[\begin{equation} \bm{L} = \begin{bmatrix} \textm{Diag}(\bm{B}\bm{1}) & -\bm{B}\\ -\bm{B}^\T & \textm{Diag}(\bm{B}^\T\bm{1}) \end{bmatrix}, \tag{5.10} \end{equation}\] where \(\bm{B} \in \R\_+^{r\times q}\) contains the edge weights between the two types of nodes (with \(r\) and \(q\) denoting the number of nodes in each group). * *Bipartite graphs from sparse GMRFs*: Consider now the sparse GMRF formulation in (5.7), but enforcing the bipartite structure with (5.10) as follows (Cardoso et al., 2022a): \[\begin{equation} \begin{array}{ll} \underset{\bm{L}\succeq\bm{0}, \bm{B}}{\textm{maximize}} & \textm{log gdet}(\bm{L}) - \textm{Tr}(\bm{L}\bm{S}) - \rho\|\bm{L}\|\_{0,\textm{off}}\\ \textm{subject to} & \bm{L} = \begin{bmatrix} \textm{Diag}(\bm{B}\bm{1}) & -\bm{B}\\ -\bm{B}^\T & \textm{Diag}(\bm{B}^\T\bm{1}) \end{bmatrix},\\ & \bm{B} \geq \bm{0}, \quad \bm{B}\bm{1}=\bm{1}. #### Isolated Nodes in Low-Rank Designs for \(k\)-Component Graphs. Isolated nodes is an artifact that may happen when imposing a low-rank structure in the Laplacian matrix to obtain a graph with clusters. Basically, if one enforces a low-rank structure to learn a \(k\)-component graph but the graph deviates from a \(k\)-component graph, the solution to this formulation may trivially leave some nodes without any connection to other nodes (i.e., isolated nodes) to artificially increase the number of clusters. Effect of isolated nodes on low-rank (clustered) financial graphs.

results.title: Tensor nonconvex unified prior for tensor recovery - ScienceDirect
results.content: Inspired by recent notable works, this paper proposes a novel tensor non-convex unified prior term, which employs weighted tensor Schatten *p*-norm as a rank surrogate function in the gradient domain. The new prior can yield a regularizer that effectively captures low-rankness and smoothness, and is applied to tensor completion and tensor robust principal component analysis models. Existing studies show that global low-rankness is one of the most typical priors, and low-rank tensor representation has become a main idea in model-based optimization methods. Besides the global low-rankness prior, a local smoothness is also significant for many tensor data, such as HSI, which has smoothing characteristics in the spatial domain. By combining smoothness prior with low-rankness prior, there appear a great amount of works that exhibit remarkable performance in tensor recovery tasks. [19] proposed a new regularization term, named tensor correlated total variation (t-CTV), which simultaneously encodes both low-rankness and smoothness priors of a tensor by introducing tensor nuclear norm (TNN) in the gradient domain, and theoretically provided a proof of exact recovery guarantee for the model. Considering the mentioned above, in this paper, we leverage t-SVD decomposition framework, which has good performance in capturing spatial correlation and retaining the intrinsic structure of data [20], and propose a novel tensor nonconvex unified prior for tensor recovery. The proposed unified prior could increase the shrinkage of small singular values while decreasing the shrinkage of large singular values when dealing with tensor recovery tasks, and could jointly characterize the global low-rankness and local smoothness of the tensor data to tackle the challenge of adjusting too many parameters. In the framework of high-order t-SVD, we propose a novel tensor nonconvex unified prior term by introducing weighted tensor Schatten *p*-norm () to improve the low-rankness/smoothness representation of tensor data in the gradient domain. In Section 2, we briefly review a number of related work about using low-rankness and smoothness priors to solve tensor recovery tasks. As the two most prominent priors in tensor data analysis, global low-rankness and local smoothness are widely employed in tensor recovery tasks. Aiming at characterizing low-rankness and smoothness of tensor, this paper introduces a tensor nonconvex unified prior (t-NUP) by employing weighted tensor Schatten *p*-norm as a rank surrogate function in the gradient domain.

Considering the variations among singular values, nonconvex regularizations have been proposed to approximate the tensor rank function more effectively, leading to improved recovery performance. In order to better simultaneously represent the global low-rank property and local smoothness of tensors, we propose a novel regularization, the Tensor-Correlated Total Variation (TCTV), based on the nonconvex Geman norm and total variation. For observation tensors with massive amounts of information loss, this issue is often solved using tensor recovery methods based on low-rank tensor priors, leading to the formulation of tensor completion models (TC) [5,6]. results.title: Infrared small target detection using the global low-rank and local smoothness coupled representation with local structure - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Infrared small target detection using the global low-rank and local smoothness coupled representation with local structure☆. This is because the low-rank and smoothness of the background exhibit inherent coupling properties. It is usually difficult to accurately fit complicated background using a single regularization term or their additive hybrid model. This paper tackles this issue by proposing a coupled tensor model that incorporates global low-rank and local smoothness. Furthermore, to suppress potential “grid artifacts”, which are usually brought on by the infrared device’s pixel array characteristics and total variation, another regularization term that focuses on the minimum absolute structure of the tensor’s gradient in the local region is constructed. Finally, comparative experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing state-of-the-art LRSD methods in terms of suppressing complicated background and sparse “grid artifacts”. Additionally, small target detection is hampered to differing degrees of interference by the intricate and diverse application scenarios as well as the inherent properties of infrared equipment.
